Chapter 1

Why Statistics Matters and Why You Already Know More Than You Think

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
• Explain why statistical literacy is essential for every researcher
• Identify everyday situations where you already use statistical thinking
• Distinguish between descriptive and inferential statistics
• Describe the role statistics plays in the research process
• Overcome common anxieties about learning statistics

1.1 Statistics Is Everywhere

You already think statistically more often than you realise. When you check weather forecasts, compare prices, judge whether a restaurant review is reliable, or decide whether a health claim is trustworthy, you are making informal statistical judgements about data, probability, and evidence. Statistics as a discipline simply formalises this everyday reasoning, giving you precise tools to answer questions like "Is this difference real or just a coincidence?" and "How confident can I be in this conclusion?" (Field, 2018).

For researchers, statistical literacy is not optional. Peer-reviewed journals require statistical evidence to support claims. Funding bodies require sample size justifications. Ethical review boards require power analyses. And readers of your research need to see that your conclusions are supported by appropriate analyses. A researcher who cannot engage with statistics is like a carpenter who cannot use a tape measure: they may have excellent ideas, but they lack the tools to execute them properly (Agresti and Finlay, 2018).

1.2 Descriptive vs. Inferential Statistics

Statistics serves two broad purposes. Descriptive statistics summarise and describe the data you have collected: What is the average score? How spread out are the values? What does the distribution look like? Inferential statistics use the data from your sample to draw conclusions about a larger population: Is the difference between two groups likely to exist in the population, or could it be due to chance? (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

Descriptive statistics are the foundation. Before you can test hypotheses or build models, you need to know what your data look like. Means, standard deviations, frequencies, and graphs provide this foundational understanding. Inferential statistics build on this foundation, using probability theory to bridge the gap between what you observed in your sample and what you want to conclude about the population (Field, 2018).

1.3 The Statistical Mindset

The statistical mindset involves accepting that variability is inherent in all data. No two people are identical. No measurement is perfectly precise. No sample perfectly represents its population. Statistics provides the tools for working productively with this variability rather than pretending it does not exist. The key concepts of this mindset, including uncertainty, probability, and evidence, will recur throughout this book (Agresti and Finlay, 2018).

Many students approach statistics with anxiety, convinced that they "aren't maths people." This anxiety is understandable but misplaced. Modern statistical practice relies more on conceptual understanding and software skills than on manual computation. You need to understand what a test does and when to use it, not how to calculate it by hand. This book focuses on understanding, application, and interpretation rather than mathematical derivation (Field, 2018).

1.4 Statistics in the Research Process

Statistics is not an afterthought to be addressed once the data have been collected. Statistical thinking should inform every stage of the research process: the formulation of research questions (which determines the type of analysis), the design of the study (which determines the type of data collected), the determination of sample size (which determines whether the study has adequate power), the collection and cleaning of data, and the analysis and interpretation of results (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

1.5 What This Book Will and Will Not Cover

This book covers the statistical methods most commonly used in social, behavioural, and health research: descriptive statistics, t-tests, ANOVA, correlation, regression, chi-square tests, and non-parametric alternatives. It also covers essential topics such as power analysis, reliability analysis, and factor analysis. Advanced topics such as structural equation modelling, multilevel modelling, and Bayesian statistics are beyond the scope of this introductory text but are briefly introduced where relevant (Field, 2018).

1.6 Chapter Summary

Statistics is an essential tool for researchers that formalises the everyday reasoning you already use. Descriptive statistics summarise your data; inferential statistics allow you to draw conclusions about populations from samples. Statistical thinking should inform every stage of the research process, from question formulation to results interpretation. This book prioritises conceptual understanding and practical application over mathematical derivation, making statistics accessible to researchers at all levels of mathematical comfort.

Methodological Debates and Advanced Theoretical Considerations

In contemporary academic discourse, the concepts and practices associated with chapter 1: why statistics matters and why you already know more than you think are subject to extensive theoretical and methodological debate. Scholars increasingly challenge traditional dogmas, asking whether established conventions adequately address emerging scientific challenges in quantitative statistics and data analysis. A central tension exists between rigid procedural compliance and adaptive intellectual flexibility. Methodological purists contend that standardisation is the only guarantor of scientific replicability, while pragmatic scholars argue that overly rigid guidelines blind researchers to contextual complexities that evade standard taxonomies.

Furthermore, rapid technological transformations, including the integration of generative artificial intelligence and high-throughput analytical platforms, are reshaping scholarly expectations. Researchers are challenged to maintain methodological transparency, verify automated outputs, and ensure that human judgment remains central to the research process. Navigating these debates requires profound methodological literacy: the ability to select appropriate tools, defend design decisions against hostile reviewer critiques, and situate your empirical claims within broader philosophical frameworks.

Inferential Statistical Test Selection Architecture

1. Research Question

Identify relationships, differences, or predictions

➔

2. Variables & Levels

Classify nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio data

➔

3. Sample Design

Independent groups vs repeated measures

➔

4. Check Assumptions

Normality, homoscedasticity, linearity

➔

5. Execute Test

Run parametric or non-parametric test

➔

6. Interpret & Report

Report test statistic, p-value, and effect size

To navigate the decision space governing chapter 1: why statistics matters and why you already know more than you think, researchers must systematically evaluate competing approaches. The following comparative matrix outlines key trade-offs, analytical requirements, and best-practice considerations:

Step-by-Step Practical Demonstration and Worked Example

To bridge theoretical principles and empirical execution, consider the following real-world worked demonstration illustrating the rigorous application of chapter 1: why statistics matters and why you already know more than you think:

A researcher examined whether an online study app improved exam scores compared to traditional studying. Group A (app, n = 35) had M = 78.4, SD = 8.2; Group B (traditional, n = 35) had M = 71.2, SD = 9.1. An independent samples t-test revealed a statistically significant difference: t(68) = 3.48, p = .001. Rather than stopping at the p-value, the researcher calculated Cohen's d = (78.4 - 71.2) / 8.66 = 0.83, indicating a large practical effect size. This demonstrates that statistical significance confirms whether an effect exists, while effect size measures how much it matters in practice (Field, 2018).

This demonstration highlights the critical importance of procedural discipline, iterative verification, and transparent reporting. In experienced academic practice, methodological decisions are never treated as mere administrative checkboxes; they represent substantive theoretical commitments that dictate the credibility and reach of your scholarship.

Reflective Discussion Prompts for Seminars and Supervisory Consultations

Use the following discussion prompts during doctoral seminars, research team meetings, or supervisory sessions to interrogate your research design:

Prompt 1: Disciplinary Norms vs. Methodological Rigour. How do prevailing conventions in your specific discipline support or hinder the rigorous execution of chapter 1: why statistics matters and why you already know more than you think? Where you identify tensions, how will you defend your chosen approach to external examiners or journal reviewers?

Prompt 2: Threats to Validity and Mitigation. What are the most severe threats to internal, external, or construct validity in your study, and what specific procedural safeguards have you implemented to counteract them?

Prompt 3: Ethical Boundaries and Transparency. How do your data collection and reporting protocols safeguard participant dignity, data security, and scholarly integrity throughout the lifecycle of this project?

Prompt 4: Long-Term Knowledge Contribution. Beyond immediate academic metrics, how does your approach to this topic contribute to enduring theoretical advancement or practical societal change?

Advanced Field Case Study: Resolving Complex Empirical Dilemmas

Case Study Analysis: Navigating High-Stakes Methodological Challenges
Context: A doctoral candidate, Marcus, tested employee productivity data across 4 departments. A standard one-way ANOVA indicated p = .03. However, Levene's test for equality of variances was violated (p = .008), rendering standard ANOVA unreliable.
Strategy: Marcus applied Welch's robust ANOVA and the Games-Howell post-hoc test, which do not assume equal variances.
Outcome: Welch's F(3, 41.2) = 4.12, p = .012 remained statistically significant. By defending the robust analytical correction in his dissertation, Marcus prevented committee critique and demonstrated high statistical competence (Tabachnick and Fidell, 2019).

Key Takeaways and Master Diagnostic Audit Checklist

Diagnostic Audit Checklist: Chapter 1: Why Statistics Matters and Why You Already Know More Than You Think

Design & Preparation Protocol

✓ Explicit justification for design choice grounded in literature
✓ Thorough pre-testing, piloting, or calibration completed
✓ Formal institutional ethical approval and consent secured
✓ Complete alignment between research questions and analytical tests

Execution & Reporting Protocol

✓ Transparent documentation enabling full independent replicability
✓ Assumption testing and outlier screening rigorously documented
✓ Exact metrics, confidence intervals, and effect sizes reported
✓ Explicit discussion of study limitations and theoretical boundaries

Glossary of Key Methodological Terms

Type I Error (α): Rejecting a true null hypothesis (false positive), typically controlled by setting the alpha threshold at .05 or .01.

Type II Error (β): Failing to reject a false null hypothesis (false negative), inversely related to statistical power (1 - β).

Statistical Power: The probability of detecting a true effect when one exists, with .80 considered the standard benchmark in social and health sciences.

Effect Size: A quantitative measure of the magnitude of an experimental effect or relationship, independent of sample size (e.g. Cohen's d, r, η²).

Homoscedasticity: The assumption that the variance of error terms is constant across all levels of the independent variables (tested via Levene's or Breusch-Pagan test).

Confidence Interval (CI): The estimated range of plausible values likely to contain the true population parameter at a specified confidence level (e.g., 95%).

Advanced Practical Exercises and Problem-Solving Scenarios

To consolidate your quantitative analytical competencies in relation to chapter 1: why statistics matters and why you already know more than you think, work through the following three applied problem-solving scenarios. Each scenario is designed to cultivate critical thinking regarding statistical decision-making, assumption diagnostics, and output interpretation.

Problem-Solving Scenario 1: Diagnostic Evaluation

Scenario 1.1: Evaluating Skewness and Kurtosis in Clinical Data

A clinical psychologist tests a new cognitive therapy across 48 patients. The dependent variable (depression score) shows a mean of 22.4, standard deviation of 6.8, skewness of +1.84 (SE = 0.34), and kurtosis of +3.92 (SE = 0.67). The Shapiro-Wilk test yields W = 0.84, p < .001.
Task & Guidance: Calculate the z-scores for skewness (1.84 / 0.34 = 5.41) and kurtosis (3.92 / 0.67 = 5.85). Since both z-scores exceed the critical threshold of ±3.29 (for moderate samples), the normality assumption is severely violated. Formulate a dual-path solution: (a) apply a logarithmic or square-root transformation, or (b) select the appropriate non-parametric alternative (Mann-Whitney U or Wilcoxon test) and justify your choice in a thesis methodology section (Field, 2018).

Problem-Solving Scenario 2: Effect Size and Statistical Power

Scenario 1.2: Decoupling Sample Size from Substantive Magnitude

An educational researcher compares reading comprehension across two classrooms (N = 800 per group). An independent t-test yields t(1598) = 2.15, p = .031. The mean difference is 0.8 points on a 100-point test (Group 1: M = 74.2; Group 2: M = 73.4; Pooled SD = 7.4).
Task & Guidance: While p < .05, calculate Cohen's d: d = 0.8 / 7.4 = 0.11. By Cohen's benchmarks, an effect size of 0.11 is negligible (< 0.20). Write a critical interpretation explaining why a massive sample size produced a statistically significant result for a practically meaningless educational intervention, demonstrating why effect size reporting is essential (Ellis, 2010).

Problem-Solving Scenario 3: Assumption Diagnostics in Multivariable Models

Scenario 1.3: Diagnosing Multicollinearity in Multiple Regression

A researcher regresses job performance on three predictors: Job Satisfaction, Organizational Commitment, and Employee Engagement. The overall model is significant (R² = .54, F(3, 146) = 57.1, p < .001), but none of the individual predictor coefficients reach statistical significance (all p > .15). Collinearity diagnostics reveal Variance Inflation Factors (VIF) of 9.4, 11.2, and 12.8.
Task & Guidance: Identify the diagnostic failure: severe multicollinearity (VIF > 10). The predictors are so heavily inter-correlated that the regression algorithm cannot isolate their unique predictive variance. Outline the corrective strategy: composite variable creation via exploratory factor analysis or removing redundant redundant predictor variables (Tabachnick and Fidell, 2019).

Chapter 2

Variables, Scales of Measurement, and Data Types

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
• Define and classify variables as independent, dependent, or control

• Identify continuous and categorical data types
• Explain why the level of measurement determines the appropriate statistical test

2.1 What Is a Variable?

A variable is any characteristic, attribute, or quantity that can take on different values across individuals or observations. Age, gender, income, test scores, satisfaction ratings, and treatment group are all variables. In research, we distinguish between independent variables (the factors we manipulate or use to predict), dependent variables (the outcomes we measure), and control variables (the factors we hold constant or adjust for to isolate the relationship of interest) (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

The distinction between independent and dependent variables is fundamental to research design and statistical analysis. The independent variable is the presumed cause or predictor; the dependent variable is the presumed effect or outcome. In an experiment studying the effect of a teaching method on exam scores, the teaching method is the independent variable and the exam score is the dependent variable. The choice of statistical test depends in part on whether the independent and dependent variables are categorical or continuous (Field, 2018).

2.2 Scales of Measurement

Stevens (1946) identified four scales of measurement, each with different properties and different implications for statistical analysis. Nominal scales classify observations into categories without any order: gender, ethnicity, marital status. Ordinal scales rank observations in order but without equal intervals: educational level (primary, secondary, tertiary), satisfaction ratings (dissatisfied, neutral, satisfied). Interval scales have equal intervals between values but no true zero: temperature in Celsius, IQ scores. Ratio scales have equal intervals and a true zero: age, income, height, weight (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

The scale of measurement determines which statistical operations are meaningful. You can calculate a mean for interval and ratio data but not for nominal data. You can rank ordinal data but cannot meaningfully calculate the difference between ranks. Applying an inappropriate statistical method to the wrong type of data produces results that are technically calculable but substantively meaningless (Field, 2018).

2.3 Continuous vs. Categorical Variables

A simpler but equally useful classification divides variables into continuous and categorical types. Continuous variables can take any value within a range: age, weight, temperature, score. Categorical variables assign observations to groups or categories: gender, treatment group, nationality. Some variables fall in between: a five-point Likert scale produces ordinal data that is sometimes treated as continuous for analytical convenience, a practice that is debated but widely accepted when certain conditions are met (Agresti and Finlay, 2018).

2.4 Why This Matters for Choosing a Test

The type of independent and dependent variable determines which statistical test is appropriate. A continuous dependent variable and a categorical independent variable with two groups calls for a t-test. A continuous dependent variable and a categorical independent variable with three or more groups calls for ANOVA. Two continuous variables call for correlation or regression. Two categorical variables call for a chi-square test. This matching of variable types to statistical tests is one of the most important practical skills in statistics (Field, 2018).

Continuous IV × Continuous DV

Continuous IV × Categorical DV

Logistic regression

Understanding variables, scales of measurement, and data types is the essential prerequisite for choosing and interpreting statistical tests. Chapter 3

Descriptive Statistics: Summarising Your Data at a Glance

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
• Calculate and interpret measures of central tendency: mean, median, and mode
• Calculate and interpret measures of dispersion: range, variance, and standard deviation
• Create and interpret frequency tables and distributions
• Identify skewness and kurtosis in data distributions
• Select the appropriate descriptive statistics for different variable types

3.1 Measures of Central Tendency

Measures of central tendency summarise a distribution with a single value that represents the "centre" of the data. The three most common measures are the mean (arithmetic average), the median (the middle value when data are ordered), and the mode (the most frequently occurring value). Each has strengths and limitations, and the choice among them depends on the scale of measurement and the shape of the distribution (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

The mean is the most widely used measure and is appropriate for interval and ratio data with approximately symmetric distributions. The median is preferred when the distribution is skewed, because it is not affected by extreme values. The mode is the only appropriate measure of central tendency for nominal data. For ordinal data, the median is typically the most appropriate measure. Understanding which measure to use and why is one of the first practical skills in statistical analysis (Field, 2018).

3.2 Measures of Dispersion

While central tendency tells you where the centre of the data is, measures of dispersion tell you how spread out the data are. The range (the difference between the highest and lowest values) is the simplest measure but is sensitive to outliers. The variance (the average of the squared deviations from the mean) quantifies the overall spread of the data. The standard deviation (the square root of the variance) is expressed in the same units as the original data, making it more interpretable than the variance (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

The interquartile range (IQR), the difference between the 75th and 25th percentiles, is a robust alternative that is less affected by outliers. It is particularly useful for skewed distributions and ordinal data. Reporting both a measure of central tendency and a measure of dispersion gives a much more complete picture of the data than reporting either alone (Field, 2018).

3.3 Frequency Tables and Distributions

A frequency table shows how many times each value or category appears in the dataset. For categorical variables, it lists each category and its count and percentage. For continuous variables, values are typically grouped into intervals (bins) to create a frequency distribution. Histograms provide a visual representation of frequency distributions, showing the shape of the data at a glance (Agresti and Finlay, 2018).

3.4 Skewness and Kurtosis

Skewness measures the asymmetry of a distribution. A positively skewed distribution has a long tail to the right (e.g., income data, where most people earn moderate amounts and a few earn very high amounts). A negatively skewed distribution has a long tail to the left. Kurtosis measures the "peakedness" of a distribution relative to the normal distribution. High kurtosis (leptokurtic) indicates more extreme values than expected; low kurtosis (platykurtic) indicates fewer extreme values (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

Skewness and kurtosis are important because many statistical tests assume that the data are approximately normally distributed. When data are substantially skewed, the mean may be misleading, and parametric tests may produce inaccurate results. Checking for skewness and kurtosis is an essential step in data screening before analysis (Field, 2018).

3.5 Visualising Descriptive Statistics

Effective data visualisation is an essential complement to numerical descriptive statistics. Bar charts display the frequencies or means of categorical variables. Histograms display the distribution of continuous variables. Box plots display the median, quartiles, and outliers. Scatter plots display the relationship between two continuous variables. Each type of visualisation serves a specific purpose, and choosing the right one depends on the type of data and the question being asked (Agresti and Finlay, 2018).

3.6 Chapter Summary

Descriptive statistics provide the foundation for all subsequent analysis. Measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode) and dispersion (range, standard deviation, IQR) summarise the key features of a distribution. Frequency tables, histograms, and other visualisations reveal the shape and characteristics of the data. Checking for skewness, kurtosis, and outliers is essential before proceeding to inferential analysis. Every results section should begin with descriptive statistics that give the reader a clear picture of the data.

4.1 The Bell Curve

The normal distribution, often called the bell curve, is the most important probability distribution in statistics. It is symmetric, with the mean, median, and mode all at the centre. Approximately 68% of the data fall within one standard deviation of the mean, 95% within two standard deviations, and 99.7% within three standard deviations. This 68-95-99.7 rule provides a quick way to assess how unusual a particular value is (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

Many natural phenomena produce approximately normal distributions: heights, weights, blood pressure measurements, IQ scores, and measurement errors all tend to cluster around a central value with decreasing frequency at the extremes. This ubiquity is not a coincidence; it is a consequence of the central limit theorem, which guarantees that the sum or average of a large number of independent random variables will be approximately normally distributed, regardless of the shape of the individual distributions (Field, 2018).

4.2 The Central Limit Theorem

The central limit theorem (CLT) is arguably the most important theorem in statistics. It states that the distribution of sample means approaches a normal distribution as the sample size increases, regardless of the shape of the population distribution. This means that even if the underlying data are skewed or bimodal, the average of a sufficiently large sample will be normally distributed. The CLT is the theoretical foundation for most inferential statistics, including confidence intervals and hypothesis tests (Agresti and Finlay, 2018).

4.3 Z-Scores and Standardisation

A z-score expresses how many standard deviations a value is above or below the mean. It is calculated by subtracting the mean from the value and dividing by the standard deviation: z = (X - μ) / σ. Z-scores allow comparisons across variables with different units and scales. A student with a z-score of 1.5 on an exam performed 1.5 standard deviations above the mean, regardless of the scale of the exam (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

The standard normal distribution (with mean 0 and standard deviation 1) has been tabulated to show the probability of obtaining a z-score at or below any given value. Chapter 5

Sampling, Estimation, and Confidence Intervals

Learning Objectives

• Explain the concept of a sampling distribution

• Construct and interpret confidence intervals for means and proportions
• Explain what a 95% confidence interval actually means
• Identify factors that affect the width of a confidence interval

5.1 From Sample to Population

The fundamental challenge of inferential statistics is using information from a sample to draw conclusions about a population. The sample mean is an estimate of the population mean, but it is only an estimate: a different sample from the same population would produce a different sample mean. The question is how close the sample mean is likely to be to the true population mean (Agresti and Finlay, 2018).

5.2 The Sampling Distribution

The sampling distribution of a statistic is the distribution of that statistic across all possible samples of a given size from the population. The sampling distribution of the mean, thanks to the central limit theorem, is approximately normal for large samples, with its mean equal to the population mean and its standard deviation (called the standard error) equal to the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size. The standard error quantifies the precision of the sample mean as an estimate of the population mean (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

5.3 Confidence Intervals

A confidence interval provides a range of plausible values for the population parameter based on the sample data. A 95% confidence interval for the mean is constructed by taking the sample mean and adding and subtracting 1.96 standard errors. The correct interpretation is: if we were to draw many samples and construct a 95% confidence interval from each, approximately 95% of those intervals would contain the true population mean. A common misconception is that there is a 95% probability that the population mean falls within a specific interval; in fact, the population mean is fixed, and it is the interval that varies across samples (Field, 2018).

5.4 Factors Affecting Interval Width

Three factors determine the width of a confidence interval: the confidence level (higher confidence requires a wider interval), the sample size (larger samples produce narrower intervals), and the variability of the data (more variable data produce wider intervals). Researchers can narrow their confidence intervals by increasing the sample size or by reducing measurement error, but they cannot narrow them by choosing a lower confidence level without accepting greater risk of missing the true value (Agresti and Finlay, 2018).

Confidence intervals provide more information than p-values alone. While a p-value tells you only whether the result is statistically significant, a confidence interval tells you the direction of the effect, its estimated magnitude, and the precision of the estimate. Many journals now require confidence intervals in addition to or instead of p-values, reflecting a growing recognition that interval estimation is more informative than dichotomous significance testing (Cumming, 2014).

Confidence intervals are the bridge between sample statistics and population parameters. They provide a range of plausible values for the population parameter, quantifying both the estimate and its uncertainty. Chapter 6

Hypothesis Testing: The Logic of Statistical Decisions

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
• State null and alternative hypotheses for common research questions
• Describe the four steps of hypothesis testing
• Distinguish between one-tailed and two-tailed tests
• Explain Type I and Type II errors

6.1 The Logic of the Test

Hypothesis testing is a formal procedure for using sample data to evaluate a claim about a population. The logic is indirect: we start by assuming the null hypothesis is true (typically that there is no effect or no difference), calculate the probability of obtaining data as extreme as or more extreme than what we observed under this assumption, and then decide whether this probability is small enough to reject the null hypothesis in favour of the alternative (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

6.2 Null and Alternative Hypotheses

The null hypothesis (H₀) states that there is no effect, no difference, or no relationship. The alternative hypothesis (H₁ or Hₐ) states that there is an effect, a difference, or a relationship. The null hypothesis is the default position; the burden of proof rests on the alternative hypothesis. We never "prove" the null hypothesis; we either reject it (if the evidence is strong enough) or fail to reject it (if the evidence is insufficient) (Field, 2018).

6.3 The Four Steps

Hypothesis testing follows four steps: (1) State the hypotheses (null and alternative). (2) Set the significance level (α), typically 0.05. (3) Calculate the test statistic and its associated p-value. (4) Make a decision: if the p-value is less than α, reject the null hypothesis; otherwise, fail to reject it. These steps provide a structured framework for making evidence-based decisions (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

6.4 Type I and Type II Errors

A Type I error occurs when we reject a true null hypothesis (a false positive). The probability of a Type I error is equal to the significance level α. A Type II error occurs when we fail to reject a false null hypothesis (a false negative). The probability of a Type II error is denoted β, and statistical power is 1 − β. Researchers must balance the risk of both types of error: a very strict significance level (such as 0.001) reduces the risk of Type I error but increases the risk of Type II error (Field, 2018).

6.5 One-Tailed vs. Two-Tailed Tests

A two-tailed test evaluates whether the effect is in either direction (greater or less than expected). A one-tailed test evaluates whether the effect is in a specific, pre-specified direction. One-tailed tests have more statistical power for detecting effects in the predicted direction but cannot detect effects in the opposite direction. 7.1 What a p-Value Really Means

A p-value is the probability of obtaining results as extreme as or more extreme than those observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the results occurred by chance. And it is not the probability that you will make an error if you reject the null hypothesis. These common misconceptions lead to widespread misinterpretation of statistical results (Wasserstein and Lazar, 2016).

A small p-value (such as p < 0.05) indicates that the observed data are unlikely under the null hypothesis, which provides evidence against the null hypothesis. A large p-value indicates that the data are consistent with the null hypothesis but does not prove that the null hypothesis is true: the data may also be consistent with many alternative hypotheses (Agresti and Finlay, 2018).

7.2 The Problem with the 0.05 Threshold

The conventional threshold of p < 0.05 for declaring statistical significance is arbitrary and has been criticised for encouraging dichotomous thinking (significant vs. non-significant) when evidence actually exists on a continuum. A result with p = 0.049 is treated as "significant" while p = 0.051 is "non-significant," even though the two results are virtually identical in their evidential strength. This arbitrary boundary has contributed to problems such as p-hacking, in which researchers manipulate their analyses to achieve p < 0.05 (Wasserstein and Lazar, 2016).

7.3 Effect Sizes

Effect sizes quantify the magnitude of an effect independently of sample size. While a p-value tells you whether an effect is statistically significant, the effect size tells you how large the effect is. With a large enough sample, even a trivially small difference can be statistically significant. Effect sizes provide the information needed to evaluate the practical significance of a finding (Cohen, 1992).

Chapter 8

Statistical Power and Sample Size Planning

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
• Define statistical power and explain its importance
• Identify the four factors that determine power
• Conduct a basic power analysis for common tests
• Use G*Power or similar software for sample size calculations
• Justify your sample size in a research proposal

8.1 What Is Statistical Power?

Statistical power is the probability that a study will detect a true effect when one exists. It is the complement of the Type II error rate: Power = 1 − β. A study with power of 0.80 has an 80% chance of detecting a true effect and a 20% chance of missing it. Underpowered studies waste resources and risk producing false negative results that may discourage further research on effective interventions (Cohen, 1992).

8.2 The Four Determinants of Power

Power is determined by four factors: sample size (larger samples have more power), effect size (larger effects are easier to detect), significance level (more lenient criteria provide more power), and variability (less noisy data provide more power). Of these, sample size is the factor most directly under the researcher's control. Power analysis uses the other three factors to calculate the minimum sample size needed to achieve adequate power (Field, 2018).

8.3 Conducting a Power Analysis

A power analysis should be conducted during the study design phase, before data collection begins. The researcher specifies the expected effect size (from prior research or pilot data), the desired power level (conventionally 0.80), and the significance level (conventionally 0.05). Software such as G*Power then calculates the minimum required sample size. Power analyses should be reported in research proposals and in the methodology section of published papers (Cohen, 1992).

8.4 What If I Don't Know the Effect Size?

Estimating the expected effect size is often the most challenging aspect of power analysis. Sources of estimates include published meta-analyses, prior studies on the same topic, pilot study data, and Cohen's (1992) benchmarks for small, medium, and large effects. When no prior information is available, a sensitivity analysis can show the minimum detectable effect size for different sample sizes, helping the researcher assess whether the study is likely to be informative (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

8.5 Chapter Summary

Statistical power analysis is an essential component of research design that ensures the study has a sufficient sample size to detect meaningful effects. Underpowered studies are wasteful and produce unreliable results. Power depends on sample size, effect size, significance level, and variability. Every quantitative study should include a power analysis, and the results should be reported in the methodology section to demonstrate that the sample size is adequate for the research question.

9.1 When to Use the Independent-Samples t-Test

The independent-samples t-test compares the means of two independent groups on a continuous dependent variable. It answers questions such as "Do male and female students differ in their exam scores?" or "Did the treatment group perform better than the control group?" The two groups must be independent, meaning that the participants in one group are different people from those in the other group (Field, 2018).

9.2 Assumptions

The independent-samples t-test assumes that the dependent variable is continuous and approximately normally distributed within each group, that the two groups are independent, and that the variances of the two groups are approximately equal (homogeneity of variances). Normality can be assessed using histograms, Q-Q plots, or the Shapiro-Wilk test. Homogeneity of variances can be assessed using Levene's test. When variances are unequal, Welch's t-test provides a robust alternative that does not assume equal variances (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

9.3 Conducting the Test

The t-statistic is calculated as the difference between the two group means divided by the standard error of the difference. The standard error reflects the variability of the difference between means across samples. A large t-value indicates that the difference between the groups is large relative to the variability, providing evidence against the null hypothesis of no difference (Field, 2018).

Cohen's d quantifies the size of the difference between two groups in standard deviation units. It is calculated by dividing the difference between the group means by the pooled standard deviation. The Paired-Samples t-Test

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

• Identify when the paired-samples t-test is appropriate
• Conduct and interpret the test
• Calculate the effect size for paired designs
• Report results in APA format

10.1 When to Use the Paired-Samples t-Test

The paired-samples t-test (also called the dependent-samples or related-samples t-test) compares the means of two related measurements. The most common applications are pre-test/post-test designs, in which the same participants are measured before and after an intervention, and matched-pairs designs, in which participants in the two groups are matched on relevant characteristics (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

10.2 The Logic of Pairing

The paired-samples t-test analyses the difference scores: for each participant, the difference between their two measurements is calculated, and the test evaluates whether the mean difference is significantly different from zero. By focusing on within-person change, the paired design eliminates individual differences from the error term, typically providing more statistical power than the independent-samples t-test (Field, 2018).

10.3 Assumptions and Conduct

The paired-samples t-test assumes that the difference scores are approximately normally distributed. With large samples, the test is robust to violations of normality. The test statistic is calculated as the mean difference divided by the standard error of the mean difference. A significant result indicates that the mean change from pre-test to post-test (or between matched pairs) is unlikely to be zero in the population (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

10.4 Effect Size and Reporting

The effect size for paired designs can be calculated as Cohen's d for paired samples, using the mean difference divided by the standard deviation of the difference scores. Alternatively, Cohen's dz (the mean difference divided by the standard deviation of differences) is commonly reported. APA format: "Anxiety scores decreased significantly from pre-test (M = 42.3, SD = 8.1) to post-test (M = 36.7, SD = 7.9), t(49) = 4.28, p < .001, d = 0.61" (APA, 2020).

The paired-samples t-test is appropriate for comparing two related measurements, most commonly in pre-test/post-test designs. Chapter 11

One-Way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
• Explain when one-way ANOVA is preferred over multiple t-tests
• State the hypotheses and assumptions of one-way ANOVA
• Interpret the F-statistic, p-value, and eta-squared
• Conduct post-hoc comparisons to identify specific group differences
• Report ANOVA results in APA format

11.1 Why Not Just Use Multiple t-Tests?

When comparing three or more groups, conducting multiple t-tests inflates the Type I error rate. With three groups, there are three pairwise comparisons; with four groups, six comparisons; with five groups, ten. Each comparison at α = 0.05 has a 5% chance of a false positive, and the cumulative risk grows rapidly. ANOVA solves this problem by testing all group differences simultaneously with a single test, maintaining the overall Type I error rate at the desired level (Field, 2018).

11.2 The Logic of ANOVA

ANOVA compares the variability between groups (how much the group means differ from each other) with the variability within groups (how much individual scores differ from their group mean). If the between-group variability is substantially larger than the within-group variability, this suggests that the group means are genuinely different, not just reflecting random variation. The ratio of between-group to within-group variability is the F-statistic (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

11.3 Assumptions

One-way ANOVA assumes that the dependent variable is continuous, that the groups are independent, that the data within each group are approximately normally distributed, and that the variances across groups are approximately equal. ANOVA is robust to moderate violations of normality, particularly with larger samples. Welch's ANOVA provides a robust alternative when the homogeneity of variances assumption is violated (Field, 2018).

11.4 Post-Hoc Comparisons

A significant F-test tells you that at least one group mean differs from the others, but it does not tell you which specific groups differ. Post-hoc comparisons, such as Tukey's HSD (honestly significant difference), Bonferroni correction, or Games-Howell test, provide pairwise comparisons while controlling the family-wise error rate. Tukey's HSD is the most commonly used post-hoc test and is appropriate when variances are equal and group sizes are similar (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

11.5 Effect Size: Eta-Squared

Eta-squared (η²) is the most common effect size for ANOVA. It represents the proportion of total variance in the dependent variable that is explained by the independent variable. Cohen's (1992) benchmarks suggest η² = 0.01 (small), 0.06 (medium), and 0.14 (large). Partial eta-squared (η²p) is often reported in factorial designs and is the default in many software packages (Field, 2018).

11.6 Chapter Summary

One-way ANOVA is the appropriate test for comparing means across three or more independent groups while controlling the Type I error rate. The F-statistic compares between-group variability to within-group variability. Post-hoc tests identify which specific groups differ. Eta-squared quantifies the effect size. Factorial ANOVA and Interaction Effects

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

• Conduct simple effects analyses when interactions are significant

12.1 What Is a Factorial Design?

A factorial design includes two or more independent variables (called factors) that are crossed, meaning every level of each factor is combined with every level of every other factor. A 2×3 factorial design has two factors: one with two levels and one with three levels, producing six conditions. Factorial designs are efficient because they allow the simultaneous examination of multiple factors and their interactions (Field, 2018).

12.2 Main Effects and Interactions

A main effect is the overall effect of one factor, averaged across levels of the other factor(s). An interaction effect occurs when the effect of one factor depends on the level of another factor. For example, if a drug is effective for young adults but not for older adults, there is an interaction between drug and age. Interactions are often the most important findings in factorial designs because they reveal the conditions under which an effect occurs (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

12.3 Interpreting Interaction Plots

Interaction plots display the means for each combination of factor levels. Non-parallel lines indicate an interaction. The greater the departure from parallelism, the stronger the interaction. When lines cross, the interaction is said to be "disordinal," meaning the effect of one factor reverses across levels of the other. When lines diverge without crossing, the interaction is "ordinal," meaning the effect is stronger at some levels than others but does not reverse (Field, 2018).

12.4 Simple Effects Analysis

When a significant interaction is found, the main effects are often misleading because they average across conditions where the effect may differ. Simple effects analysis examines the effect of one factor at each level of the other factor separately. For example, if there is a drug × age interaction, simple effects analysis would test the effect of the drug separately for young adults and older adults (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

Chapter 13

Correlation: Measuring the Strength of a Relationship

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
• Define and interpret Pearson's correlation coefficient (r)
• Identify the assumptions of Pearson's r
• Distinguish between positive, negative, and zero correlations
• Explain why correlation does not imply causation
• Use Spearman's rho for ordinal or non-normal data

13.1 What Is Correlation?

Correlation measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two continuous variables. Pearson's correlation coefficient (r) ranges from −1 to +1. A value of +1 indicates a perfect positive relationship (as one variable increases, the other increases proportionally). A value of −1 indicates a perfect negative relationship (as one increases, the other decreases proportionally). A value of 0 indicates no linear relationship (Field, 2018).

13.2 Interpreting Correlation Strength

Cohen's (1992) benchmarks suggest that r = 0.10 is a small correlation, r = 0.30 is medium, and r = 0.50 is large. However, what constitutes a "meaningful" correlation depends on the research context. In some fields, a correlation of 0.30 is considered substantial; in others, correlations of 0.70 or higher are expected. The coefficient of determination (r²) indicates the proportion of variance in one variable that is shared with the other: r = 0.50 means r² = 0.25, indicating that 25% of the variance is shared (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

13.3 Assumptions and Alternatives

Pearson's r assumes that both variables are continuous and normally distributed, that the relationship is linear, and that there are no extreme outliers. When these assumptions are violated, Spearman's rank correlation (ρ or rs) provides a non-parametric alternative that measures the strength of the monotonic relationship between two variables. Spearman's correlation is based on the ranks of the data rather than the raw values and is appropriate for ordinal data or data with non-linear relationships (Field, 2018).

13.4 Correlation Does Not Imply Causation

This principle is perhaps the most important lesson in statistics. A significant correlation between two variables does not mean that one causes the other. The correlation between ice cream sales and drowning deaths does not mean that ice cream causes drowning; both are caused by a third variable (hot weather). Correlation can be due to direct causation, reverse causation, or confounding by a third variable. Only experimental designs with random assignment can establish causation (Agresti and Finlay, 2018).

13.5 Chapter Summary

Correlation is a fundamental statistical tool for measuring the strength and direction of relationships between continuous variables. Pearson's r measures linear relationships; Spearman's ρ measures monotonic relationships. While correlation is essential for identifying relationships, it cannot establish causation. Researchers must always consider alternative explanations for observed correlations and report both the correlation coefficient and its confidence interval.

Learning Objectives

14.1 From Correlation to Prediction

While correlation measures the strength of the relationship between two variables, regression allows prediction: given a value of the independent variable, what is the predicted value of the dependent variable? Simple linear regression fits a straight line to the data that minimises the sum of squared differences between the observed and predicted values. The equation of this line, Y = a + bX, provides the prediction model (Field, 2018).

14.2 The Regression Equation

The regression equation has two components: the intercept (a), which is the predicted value of Y when X equals zero, and the slope (b), which indicates how much Y changes for each one-unit increase in X. The slope is the heart of the regression: it quantifies the strength and direction of the relationship between the predictor and the outcome. A positive slope means Y increases as X increases; a negative slope means Y decreases as X increases (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

14.3 R-Squared

R² (the coefficient of determination) represents the proportion of variance in the dependent variable that is explained by the independent variable. An R² of 0.36 means that 36% of the variance in Y is accounted for by X. The remaining 64% is due to other factors or random variation. R² ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating a better fit. In social science research, R² values of 0.02-0.12 are common for individual predictors (Field, 2018).

Linear regression assumes that the relationship between X and Y is linear, that the residuals (the differences between observed and predicted values) are normally distributed, that the residuals have constant variance across all levels of X (homoscedasticity), and that the observations are independent. Residual plots are the primary diagnostic tool: a plot of residuals against predicted values should show no systematic pattern (Agresti and Finlay, 2018).

Chapter 15

Multiple Regression: Predicting with Several Variables

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
• Explain the purpose and logic of multiple regression

• Evaluate model fit using R² and adjusted R²
• Check for multicollinearity and other diagnostic issues
• Build a regression model using hierarchical or stepwise methods

15.1 Beyond One Predictor

Multiple regression extends simple regression by including two or more independent variables (predictors) in the model. This allows the researcher to examine the unique contribution of each predictor while controlling for the effects of the others. For example, a model predicting job satisfaction might include autonomy, pay, workload, and supervisor support as predictors, and the regression coefficients would indicate the unique effect of each predictor after controlling for the others (Field, 2018).

15.2 Interpreting Coefficients

In multiple regression, each coefficient represents the expected change in Y for a one-unit increase in the predictor, holding all other predictors constant. Unstandardised coefficients (B) are in the original units of the variables. Standardised coefficients (β) are in standard deviation units and allow direct comparison of the relative importance of different predictors: the predictor with the largest absolute β has the strongest unique relationship with the outcome (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

15.3 R² and Adjusted R²

R² in multiple regression represents the proportion of variance in the dependent variable explained by all the predictors together. Adding predictors always increases R², even if the new predictor has no real relationship with the outcome. Adjusted R² corrects for the number of predictors in the model and only increases when a new predictor improves the model more than would be expected by chance. Adjusted R² is the preferred measure of model fit in multiple regression (Field, 2018).

15.4 Multicollinearity

Multicollinearity occurs when two or more predictors are highly correlated with each other. High multicollinearity inflates the standard errors of the regression coefficients, making them unstable and difficult to interpret. Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) values above 10 (or tolerance values below 0.10) indicate problematic multicollinearity. Solutions include removing one of the correlated predictors, combining them into a composite variable, or using techniques such as principal components regression (Agresti and Finlay, 2018).

15.5 Model Building Strategies

Hierarchical regression enters predictors in blocks, with each block adding to the previous model. This approach is theory-driven and allows the researcher to test whether a set of predictors explains variance beyond what is already explained by previously entered predictors. Stepwise regression uses statistical criteria to select predictors automatically, but it is prone to capitalising on chance and producing models that do not replicate. Hierarchical regression is generally preferred in confirmatory research (Field, 2018).

15.6 Chapter Summary

Multiple regression is a powerful tool for examining the unique contributions of multiple predictors to a dependent variable. It controls for confounding by holding other predictors constant and allows comparison of relative predictor importance through standardised coefficients. Diagnostic checks for multicollinearity and residual patterns are essential for ensuring model validity. Hierarchical entry strategies provide a theory-driven approach to model building.

Chapter 16

Logistic Regression: When the Outcome Is Yes or No

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
• Identify when logistic regression is appropriate
• Interpret odds ratios and their confidence intervals
• Evaluate model fit for logistic regression models
• Distinguish between binary, ordinal, and multinomial logistic regression
• Report logistic regression results

16.1 When the Dependent Variable Is Categorical

Linear regression assumes a continuous dependent variable. When the dependent variable is categorical, particularly binary (yes/no, pass/fail, present/absent), logistic regression is the appropriate method. Instead of predicting the value of the dependent variable directly, logistic regression predicts the probability that the outcome falls in a particular category, using the logistic function to ensure that predicted probabilities fall between 0 and 1 (Field, 2018).

16.2 The Logistic Function and Odds Ratios

The logistic function transforms the linear combination of predictors into a probability. The key output of logistic regression is the odds ratio (OR) for each predictor, which indicates how much the odds of the outcome change for a one-unit increase in the predictor. An OR of 2.0 means the odds are doubled; an OR of 0.5 means the odds are halved. An OR of 1.0 means the predictor has no effect on the odds (Agresti and Finlay, 2018).

16.3 Model Fit

17.1 Testing Categorical Relationships

Chi-square tests are used when both variables are categorical. The chi-square goodness-of-fit test examines whether the observed frequencies in a single categorical variable match a hypothesised distribution. The chi-square test of independence examines whether there is a relationship between two categorical variables by comparing the observed frequencies in a contingency table with the frequencies expected under the assumption of independence (Field, 2018).

17.2 The Chi-Square Test of Independence

The test of independence compares observed cell frequencies with expected frequencies calculated under the assumption that the two variables are independent. A large chi-square statistic indicates a substantial discrepancy between observed and expected frequencies, suggesting that the variables are not independent. The degrees of freedom are (rows − 1) × (columns − 1), and the p-value indicates the probability of obtaining a discrepancy as large as or larger than the observed one if the variables were truly independent (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

Cramér's V measures the strength of association between two categorical variables. It ranges from 0 (no association) to 1 (perfect association). Chapter 18

Non-Parametric Alternatives: Mann–Whitney, Wilcoxon, and Kruskal–Wallis

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
• Identify when non-parametric tests should be used
• Apply the Mann–Whitney U test as an alternative to the independent-samples t-test
• Apply the Wilcoxon signed-rank test as an alternative to the paired-samples t-test
• Apply the Kruskal–Wallis test as an alternative to one-way ANOVA
• Report non-parametric test results

18.1 When to Go Non-Parametric

Non-parametric tests make fewer assumptions about the data than parametric tests. They do not require normality or equal variances, and they are appropriate for ordinal data, small samples, and distributions with extreme outliers or heavy skew. The trade-off is that non-parametric tests are generally less powerful than their parametric counterparts when the parametric assumptions are met (Field, 2018).

18.2 The Mann–Whitney U Test

The Mann–Whitney U test compares two independent groups using ranked data rather than raw scores. It tests whether the distribution of ranks differs between the two groups. It is the non-parametric alternative to the independent-samples t-test and is appropriate when the dependent variable is ordinal or when the normality assumption is violated (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

18.3 The Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test

The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is the non-parametric alternative to the paired-samples t-test. It analyses the differences between paired observations, ranking the absolute values of the differences and then comparing the sum of ranks for positive and negative differences. It is appropriate for ordinal paired data or when the distribution of difference scores is non-normal (Field, 2018).

18.4 The Kruskal–Wallis Test

The Kruskal–Wallis test is the non-parametric alternative to one-way ANOVA. It compares three or more independent groups using ranked data. A significant Kruskal–Wallis test indicates that at least one group differs, and post-hoc pairwise comparisons (such as Dunn's test with Bonferroni correction) can identify which groups differ (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

18.5 Chapter Summary

Non-parametric tests provide robust alternatives to parametric tests when the data do not meet the assumptions of normality or when the variables are ordinal. The Mann–Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank, and Kruskal–Wallis tests parallel the t-tests and one-way ANOVA, using ranked data instead of raw scores. While less powerful than parametric tests when assumptions are met, they provide valid results under conditions where parametric tests may be misleading.

Chapter 19

Reliability Analysis: Cronbach's Alpha and Beyond

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

• Describe alternatives to Cronbach's alpha

19.1 What Is Reliability?

Reliability is the consistency of a measurement instrument. A reliable instrument produces similar results when administered to the same respondents under similar conditions. In survey research, reliability is most commonly assessed through internal consistency: the degree to which the items in a scale measure the same underlying construct. High internal consistency means that the items are correlated with each other, suggesting they tap into the same construct (DeVellis, 2017).

19.2 Cronbach's Alpha

Cronbach's alpha (α) is the most widely reported measure of internal consistency. It ranges from 0 to 1, with higher values indicating greater consistency. The conventional thresholds are α ≥ 0.70 for acceptable reliability, α ≥ 0.80 for good reliability, and α ≥ 0.90 for excellent reliability in research contexts. However, these thresholds are guidelines, not rigid rules, and the acceptable level depends on the purpose of the measurement (Field, 2018).

19.3 Improving Reliability

If Cronbach's alpha is below the acceptable threshold, the researcher can improve it by examining the item-total correlations: the correlation between each item and the total scale score. Items with low item-total correlations (typically below 0.30) are not contributing to the measurement of the construct and may be removed to improve reliability. The "alpha if item deleted" statistic shows how reliability would change if each item were removed, guiding decisions about item retention (DeVellis, 2017).

Cronbach's alpha has been criticised for its sensitivity to the number of items (longer scales produce higher alpha values) and for the assumption of tau-equivalence (that all items contribute equally to the construct). McDonald's omega (ω) is an alternative that does not require tau-equivalence and is increasingly recommended by methodologists. Composite reliability (CR), calculated from factor analysis results, provides another alternative (Field, 2018).

Exploratory and Confirmatory Factor Analysis

Learning Objectives

20.1 What Is Factor Analysis?

Factor analysis is a family of statistical methods used to identify the underlying structure of a set of variables. It examines the correlations among a large number of variables and identifies clusters of variables (factors) that are highly correlated with each other but relatively uncorrelated with variables in other clusters. Factors are interpreted as latent constructs that explain the observed correlations (Field, 2018).

20.2 Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA)

EFA is used when the researcher does not have a prior hypothesis about the number or nature of the underlying factors. It explores the data to identify the factor structure. Key decisions in EFA include the extraction method (principal components analysis vs. common factor analysis), the number of factors to retain (using eigenvalues, scree plots, or parallel analysis), and the rotation method (varimax for uncorrelated factors, oblimin for correlated factors) (DeVellis, 2017).

20.3 Interpreting Factor Loadings

Factor loadings indicate the strength of the relationship between each variable and each factor. Loadings above 0.40 are conventionally considered meaningful, though some researchers use a threshold of 0.30 or 0.50. Variables should load strongly on one factor and weakly on others (simple structure). Cross-loading items (those that load substantially on more than one factor) may need to be removed or reassigned (Field, 2018).

20.4 Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA)

CFA tests a pre-specified factor model against the observed data. The researcher specifies which items should load on which factors, and the analysis evaluates how well the hypothesised model fits the data. Model fit is assessed using indices such as the chi-square test, the Comparative Fit Index (CFI), the Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI), and the Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA). Good fit is indicated by CFI and TLI values above 0.95 and RMSEA values below 0.06 (Hu and Bentler, 1999).

Chapter 21

Choosing the Right Test: A Decision Flowchart

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
• Classify your research question by type: descriptive, comparative, or relational
• Identify the number and type of your variables
• Use a decision flowchart to select the appropriate statistical test
• Match common research questions to specific tests
• Avoid common mistakes in test selection

21.1 The Test Selection Process

Choosing the right statistical test is one of the most important practical skills in quantitative research. The choice depends on three factors: the type of research question (describing, comparing, or relating), the number and type of variables (categorical or continuous, independent or dependent), and the characteristics of the data (sample size, distribution, independence). A systematic approach to test selection prevents the common error of applying an inappropriate test and producing meaningless results (Field, 2018).

21.2 The Decision Flowchart

Statistical Test Decision Guide

Comparing Two Groups

Independent groups + continuous DV → Independent t-test
Related groups + continuous DV → Paired t-test
Categorical DV → Chi-square test

Comparing Three+ Groups

Independent groups + continuous DV → One-way ANOVA
Two IVs + continuous DV → Factorial ANOVA
Ordinal DV → Kruskal-Wallis

Examining Relationships

Two continuous variables → Correlation
One predictor → Simple regression
Multiple predictors → Multiple regression

Predicting Categories

Binary outcome → Binary logistic regression
Ordinal outcome → Ordinal logistic regression
Nominal outcome → Multinomial logistic regression

21.3 Common Mistakes in Test Selection

Common mistakes include using a parametric test when the data violate its assumptions, using multiple t-tests instead of ANOVA, using correlation to make causal claims, using linear regression with a categorical dependent variable, and using chi-square with continuous variables. Each of these errors produces results that are technically calculable but substantively wrong (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

21.4 When in Doubt

When the choice between tests is unclear, several strategies can help. Consult the assumptions of each potential test and assess whether your data meet them. Consider the level of measurement of your variables. Examine published studies with similar research designs to see which tests they used. And when multiple tests are potentially appropriate, running more than one and comparing results (as a sensitivity check) can increase confidence in the findings (Field, 2018).

21.5 Chapter Summary

Choosing the right statistical test is a systematic process that depends on the research question, the types of variables, and the characteristics of the data. The decision flowchart provides a practical tool for matching research questions to appropriate tests. Avoiding common mistakes in test selection ensures that your results are valid and interpretable.

22.1 Why Software Literacy Matters

Modern statistical analysis is conducted using software, and the ability to read and interpret software output is an essential skill. SPSS is the most widely used statistical package in social science research. SPSS output is organised into tables with descriptive labels. The final step in statistical analysis is translating software output into a clear, standardised written report. Chapter 23

Writing the Results Section of Your Paper

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
• Structure a results section logically and coherently
• Report descriptive statistics before inferential results
• Present statistical results in both text and tables
• Write results narratives that interpret rather than merely report numbers
• Follow APA conventions for statistical reporting

23.1 Structure and Flow

The results section should follow a logical structure that mirrors the research questions. Begin with descriptive statistics: sample characteristics, response rates, means, standard deviations, and frequencies. Then present the results of assumption checks. Finally, report the inferential analyses in the order of the research questions or hypotheses. Each analysis should be introduced with a reminder of the research question it addresses (APA, 2020).

23.2 Reporting Descriptive Statistics

Descriptive statistics provide the reader with a picture of the data before inferential results are presented. A table of descriptive statistics, including means, standard deviations, and sample sizes for each group or variable, is standard. For categorical variables, frequencies and percentages are reported. Reliability statistics (Cronbach's alpha) for scales should be reported in the results section or the methodology section (Field, 2018).

23.3 Reporting Inferential Results

Each inferential analysis should be reported with the test statistic, degrees of freedom, exact p-value, and effect size. For example: "A one-way ANOVA revealed a significant effect of teaching method on exam scores, F(2, 147) = 6.42, p = .002, η² = .08." Tables should complement, not duplicate, the text. Present detailed statistical results (such as regression coefficients for all predictors) in tables, and use the text to highlight the key findings and interpret them. Figures, such as bar charts with error bars or scatter plots with regression lines, provide visual summaries that make patterns accessible at a glance (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

Chapter 24

Common Statistical Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

Learning Objectives
By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:
• Identify the most common statistical mistakes in published research
• Recognise and avoid p-hacking and other questionable research practices
• Distinguish between absence of evidence and evidence of absence
• Apply good statistical practice throughout the research process
• Use checklists to ensure your analyses are sound

24.1 Using the Wrong Test

The most fundamental statistical mistake is applying a test that does not match the research question, the type of data, or the design of the study. Using a parametric test on heavily skewed data, using multiple t-tests instead of ANOVA, using correlation to make causal claims, or using linear regression with a binary outcome are all common errors that produce unreliable results. The decision flowchart in Chapter 21 provides a systematic safeguard against this mistake (Field, 2018).

24.2 Confusing Statistical and Practical Significance

A statistically significant result is not necessarily a practically important one. With a sufficiently large sample, even a trivially small effect can achieve statistical significance. Conversely, a non-significant result does not prove that there is no effect; it may simply reflect inadequate statistical power. Reporting effect sizes alongside p-values provides the information needed to evaluate practical significance (Cohen, 1992).

24.3 P-Hacking and HARKing

P-hacking refers to the practice of manipulating analyses, selectively reporting results, or running multiple tests until a statistically significant result is obtained. HARKing (Hypothesising After Results are Known) involves presenting post-hoc findings as though they were predicted in advance. Both practices inflate the false positive rate and undermine the credibility of research. Pre-registration of hypotheses and analysis plans is the most effective safeguard (Wasserstein and Lazar, 2016).

24.4 Ignoring Assumptions

Every statistical test has assumptions, and violating them can produce inaccurate results. Failing to check for normality, homogeneity of variances, independence, or linearity is a common error that can lead to incorrect conclusions. Assumption checking should be a routine part of every analysis, and violations should be addressed through data transformation, alternative tests, or robust methods (Gravetter and Wallnau, 2017).

24.5 A Statistical Quality Checklist

Before submitting your analyses, check the following: Have you used the right test for your data and research question? Have you checked and reported assumption tests? Have you reported exact p-values, effect sizes, and confidence intervals? Have you interpreted non-significant results as "no evidence of an effect" rather than "evidence of no effect"? Have you avoided multiple testing without correction? Have you reported all analyses, including non-significant ones? This checklist will catch the most common mistakes and improve the quality and credibility of your research (Field, 2018).

24.6 Chapter Summary

Statistical mistakes are common in published research, but most are preventable through careful attention to test selection, assumption checking, effect size reporting, and transparent analytical practices. P-hacking, HARKing, and selective reporting undermine the credibility of research and can be mitigated through pre-registration and adherence to reporting standards. A systematic quality checklist applied to every analysis ensures that common mistakes are caught before they reach the published record.

Methodological Debates and Advanced Theoretical Considerations

In contemporary academic discourse, the concepts and practices associated with chapter 24: common statistical mistakes and how to avoid them are subject to extensive theoretical and methodological debate. Scholars increasingly challenge traditional dogmas, asking whether established conventions adequately address emerging scientific challenges in quantitative statistics and data analysis. A central tension exists between rigid procedural compliance and adaptive intellectual flexibility. Methodological purists contend that standardisation is the only guarantor of scientific replicability, while pragmatic scholars argue that overly rigid guidelines blind researchers to contextual complexities that evade standard taxonomies.

Furthermore, rapid technological transformations, including the integration of generative artificial intelligence and high-throughput analytical platforms, are reshaping scholarly expectations. Researchers are challenged to maintain methodological transparency, verify automated outputs, and ensure that human judgment remains central to the research process. Navigating these debates requires profound methodological literacy: the ability to select appropriate tools, defend design decisions against hostile reviewer critiques, and situate your empirical claims within broader philosophical frameworks.

Step-by-Step Practical Demonstration and Worked Example

To bridge theoretical principles and empirical execution, consider the following real-world worked demonstration illustrating the rigorous application of chapter 24: common statistical mistakes and how to avoid them:

A researcher examined whether an online study app improved exam scores compared to traditional studying. Group A (app, n = 35) had M = 78.4, SD = 8.2; Group B (traditional, n = 35) had M = 71.2, SD = 9.1. An independent samples t-test revealed a statistically significant difference: t(68) = 3.48, p = .001. Rather than stopping at the p-value, the researcher calculated Cohen's d = (78.4 - 71.2) / 8.66 = 0.83, indicating a large practical effect size. This demonstrates that statistical significance confirms whether an effect exists, while effect size measures how much it matters in practice (Field, 2018).

This demonstration highlights the critical importance of procedural discipline, iterative verification, and transparent reporting. In experienced academic practice, methodological decisions are never treated as mere administrative checkboxes; they represent substantive theoretical commitments that dictate the credibility and reach of your scholarship.

Reflective Discussion Prompts for Seminars and Supervisory Consultations

Use the following discussion prompts during doctoral seminars, research team meetings, or supervisory sessions to interrogate your research design:

Prompt 1: Disciplinary Norms vs. Methodological Rigour. How do prevailing conventions in your specific discipline support or hinder the rigorous execution of chapter 24: common statistical mistakes and how to avoid them? Where you identify tensions, how will you defend your chosen approach to external examiners or journal reviewers?

Prompt 2: Threats to Validity and Mitigation. What are the most severe threats to internal, external, or construct validity in your study, and what specific procedural safeguards have you implemented to counteract them?

Prompt 3: Ethical Boundaries and Transparency. How do your data collection and reporting protocols safeguard participant dignity, data security, and scholarly integrity throughout the lifecycle of this project?

Prompt 4: Long-Term Knowledge Contribution. Beyond immediate academic metrics, how does your approach to this topic contribute to enduring theoretical advancement or practical societal change?

Advanced Field Case Study: Resolving Complex Empirical Dilemmas

Case Study Analysis: Navigating High-Stakes Methodological Challenges
Context: A doctoral candidate, Marcus, tested employee productivity data across 4 departments. A standard one-way ANOVA indicated p = .03. However, Levene's test for equality of variances was violated (p = .008), rendering standard ANOVA unreliable.
Strategy: Marcus applied Welch's robust ANOVA and the Games-Howell post-hoc test, which do not assume equal variances.
Outcome: Welch's F(3, 41.2) = 4.12, p = .012 remained statistically significant. By defending the robust analytical correction in his dissertation, Marcus prevented committee critique and demonstrated high statistical competence (Tabachnick and Fidell, 2019).

Glossary of Key Methodological Terms

Type I Error (α): Rejecting a true null hypothesis (false positive), typically controlled by setting the alpha threshold at .05 or .01.

Type II Error (β): Failing to reject a false null hypothesis (false negative), inversely related to statistical power (1 - β).

Statistical Power: The probability of detecting a true effect when one exists, with .80 considered the standard benchmark in social and health sciences.

Effect Size: A quantitative measure of the magnitude of an experimental effect or relationship, independent of sample size (e.g. Cohen's d, r, η²).

Homoscedasticity: The assumption that the variance of error terms is constant across all levels of the independent variables (tested via Levene's or Breusch-Pagan test).

Confidence Interval (CI): The estimated range of plausible values likely to contain the true population parameter at a specified confidence level (e.g., 95%).

Advanced Practical Exercises and Problem-Solving Scenarios

To consolidate your quantitative analytical competencies in relation to chapter 24: common statistical mistakes and how to avoid them, work through the following three applied problem-solving scenarios. Each scenario is designed to cultivate critical thinking regarding statistical decision-making, assumption diagnostics, and output interpretation.

Problem-Solving Scenario 1: Diagnostic Evaluation

Scenario 1.1: Evaluating Skewness and Kurtosis in Clinical Data

A clinical psychologist tests a new cognitive therapy across 48 patients. The dependent variable (depression score) shows a mean of 22.4, standard deviation of 6.8, skewness of +1.84 (SE = 0.34), and kurtosis of +3.92 (SE = 0.67). The Shapiro-Wilk test yields W = 0.84, p < .001.
Task & Guidance: Calculate the z-scores for skewness (1.84 / 0.34 = 5.41) and kurtosis (3.92 / 0.67 = 5.85). Since both z-scores exceed the critical threshold of ±3.29 (for moderate samples), the normality assumption is severely violated. Formulate a dual-path solution: (a) apply a logarithmic or square-root transformation, or (b) select the appropriate non-parametric alternative (Mann-Whitney U or Wilcoxon test) and justify your choice in a thesis methodology section (Field, 2018).

Problem-Solving Scenario 2: Effect Size and Statistical Power

Scenario 1.2: Decoupling Sample Size from Substantive Magnitude

An educational researcher compares reading comprehension across two classrooms (N = 800 per group). An independent t-test yields t(1598) = 2.15, p = .031. The mean difference is 0.8 points on a 100-point test (Group 1: M = 74.2; Group 2: M = 73.4; Pooled SD = 7.4).
Task & Guidance: While p < .05, calculate Cohen's d: d = 0.8 / 7.4 = 0.11. By Cohen's benchmarks, an effect size of 0.11 is negligible (< 0.20). Write a critical interpretation explaining why a massive sample size produced a statistically significant result for a practically meaningless educational intervention, demonstrating why effect size reporting is essential (Ellis, 2010).

Problem-Solving Scenario 3: Assumption Diagnostics in Multivariable Models

Scenario 1.3: Diagnosing Multicollinearity in Multiple Regression

A researcher regresses job performance on three predictors: Job Satisfaction, Organizational Commitment, and Employee Engagement. The overall model is significant (R² = .54, F(3, 146) = 57.1, p < .001), but none of the individual predictor coefficients reach statistical significance (all p > .15). Collinearity diagnostics reveal Variance Inflation Factors (VIF) of 9.4, 11.2, and 12.8.
Task & Guidance: Identify the diagnostic failure: severe multicollinearity (VIF > 10). The predictors are so heavily inter-correlated that the regression algorithm cannot isolate their unique predictive variance. Outline the corrective strategy: composite variable creation via exploratory factor analysis or removing redundant redundant predictor variables (Tabachnick and Fidell, 2019).
